entities.paper: Mapping Languages and Demographics with Georeferenced Corpora (2004.00809)

twitter_language_advantage.text: The abstract states that Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country.

discussion_fewer_missing.text: The discussion reports that Twitter has fewer missing languages than the web-crawled corpus in representing all languages produced by local populations.

regional_representation.text: The authors note that both corpora agree on predictions for Europe, parts of Africa with ground-truth data, and South America, but Twitter provides a better representation of North America and Oceania.

common_languages_caveat.text: The authors caution that many countries have only a few languages, so a high true positive rate may reflect only one or two languages; since English and Spanish are very common on Twitter, countries predominantly using these languages will have good representation by default.

partial_hypothesis_gdp.text: Regarding why Twitter and web-crawled data represent different populations, the authors suggest that Twitter data matches populations better when weighted by GDP and worse when weighted by internet-usage statistics, implying Twitter represents more wealthy populations; they also offer an alternate interpretation that their Twitter collection is based on urban areas, which tend to have wealthier populations.

false_positive_unexplained.text: The authors state that more research is needed to distinguish between immigration, tourism, and business as alternate sources of false positive languages appearing in digital data sets.
